records.query: Explain how the manual addresses safety risks associated with refueling military aircraft while their engines remain operational.
records.reference: The manual addresses safety risks associated with refueling military aircraft while their engines remain operational by outlining clear procedures to mitigate risks such as injury to or death of personnel, long-term health hazards, damage or destruction of equipment, and loss of mission effectiveness. Specific safety measures include stopping refueling if fuel vent pressure exceeds 4 PSI or if the tank pressure is in the red, monitoring the vent tank wet light for possible spills, avoiding the fuselage cooling fan to prevent equipment damage, verifying the nozzle is locked before fueling, checking the refueling probe for damage, restricting hot refueling to EA-6 aircraft at USAF bases, and prohibiting hot refueling of E-2 aircraft with folded wings.
records.answer: Hot refueling (engines running) is permitted only for approved aircraft and after SSEA-validated procedures are completed; aircraft will not be fueled without qualified, certified personnel, and aircraft technical order guidance, checklists and fueling system checklists must be available. Personnel must remain at least 10 feet from lower UHF antennas, and when notified of HF transmissions the operator must stop fuel flow, lay the deadman control on the ground, and avoid touching the aircraft skin, metal objects, or the servicing vehicle; a WARNING states that severe electrical shock and burns may result from touching equipment or aircraft during HF transmissions. Aircraft-to-aircraft refueling with engines running is further restricted to approved provider/receiver combinations per Table 6-3, and an installation certification team must certify sites and personnel, with MAJCOM directives defining procedures. records.query: Explain the engineering considerations for nozzle positioning during defueling operations based on equipment configuration and aircraft interface requirements.
records.reference: During defueling operations, the nozzle-equipped ball strainer valves must be in the correct defuel position, and nozzle strainers should be removed or reversed on all designated defuel units. The aircraft and equipment must be grounded or bonded before connecting the single nozzle to the aircraft. The ball valve strainer must be inspected and cleaned whenever the ball valve position is switched between refuel and defuel to prevent solid contaminants from entering the aircraft fuel systems or refueling vehicle components. Failure to comply may result in damage to equipment or loss of mission effectiveness.
records.answer: Nozzle selection and positioning for defueling depend on the aircraft interface: the D-2 straight throat nozzle or D-3 universal inlet nozzle is preferred for under-wing servicing, and if 45-degree D-1 nozzles are used, nozzles and hoses must be supported to prevent damage to aircraft receptacles (P506). The D-1 45-degree nozzle is acceptable for most SPR operations, especially fuselage servicing, while the straight throat D-2 is only for underwing applications unless mission essential, documented on the fuels automated system control log; the D-3 can be used on any SPR on any aircraft; C-135 and F-15 series have angled SPRs and can use D-1 or D-2, with D-2 preferred underwing to minimize stress damage to the SPR adapter. Inappropriate nozzle use has caused receptacle stress damage, fuel spills, and broken components (P609). Before pressurizing, the nozzle must be tested so it cannot be removed with the crank handle open; any nozzle that disconnects in the open position is defective and must be removed from service (P609). Nozzle strainers must be removed or reversed on designated defuel units, and ball strainer valves must be set to the defuel position and inspected/cleaned whenever switched between refuel and defuel, since the strainer is the last line of protection against solid contaminants (P499, P505, P386). The servicing crew member connects the SPR nozzle, and if equipped with a strainer coupling quick disconnect, tests its locking device for positive engagement before pressurizing (P401, P398). Do not pressurize the vehicle with the single point nozzle open and the aircraft valve in the defuel position (P505).

records.query: hydrostatic testing procedures aerospace systems
records.reference: Hydrostatic testing procedures for aerospace systems involve pressurizing the system in increments up to its maximum working pressure, holding for at least 30 minutes, and then drying with nitrogen. The procedure requires a test crew of two or more members and an inspector, along with equipment such as a hydrostatic pump (portable or remote controlled), a vacuum pump, and a CEC Moisture Monitor. Additional safety measures include inspecting welds, retesting flex hoses, and using barricades to protect personnel from rupture hazards.
records.answer: Hydrostatic testing is the preferred method for pressure and cryogenic propellant systems; pneumatic testing is allowed only with cognizant engineering and safety approval where hydrostatic testing is not possible. Every component of a high pressure system must withstand, without failure, leakage or permanent deformation, an internal hydrostatic test at 1-1/2 times the maximum allowable working pressure (P821). Hydrostatic test fluids must be compatible with the system fluid and not impact sensitive when mixed with it (CAUTION, P821). All pressure vessels, accumulators, piping, tube assemblies, valves and filters must be hydrostatically tested before installation (P821). Installed systems are classified: Class I (testable with water), Class II (tested with the service fluid), Class III (moisture-free, tested with trichloroethylene MIL-T-27602, NSN 6810-812-9181), and Class IV (cryogenic/oxidizer/lox-clean, tested with trichloroethylene at ambient or liquid nitrogen at cryogenic temperature) (P828, P827, P831, P832). For Class I systems, the test fluid is clean filtered water, or water with 0.5% sodium hydroxide, 0.5% sodium nitrite, 0.25% monosodium phosphate and 0.25% disodium phosphate for ferrous metals; the procedure pressurizes in increments of 50, 75 and 90 percent of maximum allowable working pressure, holding five minutes each, then pressurizes to maximum allowable working pressure and holds at least 30 minutes, after which the system is drained and blown down with filtered dry nitrogen (P828, P830). Remove or cap relief valves, regulators and burst diaphragms during testing; relief valves that cannot be removed must be rendered inoperable by a restraining device (P828). Gaseous systems are tested per the liquid procedure (P830, P831). Pneumatic test in lieu of hydrostatic requires cognizant safety approval, clearing personnel from the area, stepping pressure to 1-1/4 times maximum allowable working pressure, holding five minutes, then reducing to 2/3 of test pressure for inspection (WARNING: personnel must not enter until test complete or pressure is zero) (P830). After testing, leak test with the service fluid at maximum allowable working pressure and temperature (P830). Safety: do not probe for leaks with hands; use folded absorbent paper; do not weld while under pressure or with test fluid undrained, and obtain cognizant safety officer approval before welding; keep personnel and equipment out of the relief port path before releasing pressure; flanged leaks under no more than 500 PSI may be repaired (P876, P828). Testing crew requires an inspector present throughout, and a checklist filed with the test report (P828, P827).

records.query: How do pressure system design standards address the risks associated with dynamic stress phenomena like water hammer and thermal expansion in high-pressure environments?
records.reference: Pressure system design standards address risks from dynamic stress phenomena by using design features such as bends and controlled expansion to absorb stress from thermal expansion and vibration. Proper material selection, including compatibility and comparable coefficients of thermal expansion, is critical. Standards also require precise construction, including correct tube cutting and bend radii, and the use of appropriate gauges, valves, regulators, and piping. Hydrostatic and other tests are conducted to verify structural integrity and safety under operating conditions.
records.answer: Water hammer (shock): shock waves arise from sudden changes in flow, commonly rapid valve closure; high velocities and long lines produce high overpressures that can rupture lines or fail components. The system should be designed to minimize shock pressures; if the cause cannot be eliminated, protective devices such as surge suppressors should be added to bring amplitudes within piping and component pressure limits. Interlocks and valve-closure-time controls should not be the only protection against a major incident, since they may be removed later without knowledge of the effect. Pressure gauges subject to surge pressures above normal range should have a pulsation dampener, orifice plate, or similar device at the inlet. Thermal expansion and contraction: provision must be made in design for expansion/contraction of piping, equipment and fluids; relief devices should be provided in all isolable sections; piping in areas of extreme temperature change must be checked for adequate flexibility; and expansion joints must be selected and applied carefully, since wrong application can impose excessive stresses from operating pressure and bellows spring forces. Straight runs between two fixed anchors are not permitted unless expansion joints are provided, and hangers/supports must not interfere with free expansion and contraction between anchors, with spring hangers, sway bracing or vibration dampers provided where necessary. High-pressure systems must be supported rigidly enough to prevent excessive vibration and anchored to prevent undue strain. A WARNING states that failure to ensure adequate pipe supports at shear points can cause equipment damage and injury from earth tremors or blast-induced shock waves. Flexibility analysis per the ASA code Section VI is complicated and best left to a competent piping designer.

In clean work stations, parts should sit in the unobstructed clean airstream with hands downstream, parts containers kept off critical surfaces, and hand transfer minimized; transfer from hands or misused finger cots can exceed airborne contamination effects (P708). Air velocity must be checked (below 75 FPM or 25 FPM variation indicates a problem) and HEPA filters inspected for leaks through particle counts, since pinhole leaks contribute a high share of contamination (P708). records.query: Explain the primary factors that contribute to system failures during aircraft fuel servicing operations and how they interrelate with safety protocols.

(2) Fuel spills, fuel leaks, or aircraft damage from fire or impact require servicing to cease, fuel flow stopped and pressure relieved until the ARFF vehicle returns to standby (P599); operations must also stop during any fuel spill until removed or neutralized (P599). (3) Electrical power use, maintenance on electrical/fuel systems, or opening lines with flammable liquids during fueling is prohibited (P290); only aircraft switches required for servicing may be operated (P290). (4) Vehicles must not operate or pass within 25 feet of fuel vents and pressurized components, except for Boeing 747/757/777 including KC-46 underpass cases (P290). (5) Passengers may only enter or exit during fueling if a jetway is used, or if stairs are used on the opposite side with no closer than 25 feet from fuel vent outlets (P281). (6) Simultaneous fuel and oxygen servicing is not authorized (P540, P655, P641). (7) Voice contact must be maintained during the fuel transfer phase when passengers or crew are aboard (P289). (8) Ground power units and air conditioners must be connected before fuel servicing starts and remain connected until it ends (P290). (9) Refueling/aircraft servicing supervisors must verify concurrent-servicing status and timing before operations begin (P281). Interrelation: the equipment and fire-protection criteria (P290, P599) set when operations must stop, while personnel and positioning rules (P281, P290, P289) limit exposure to ignition and fuel hazards, so a component malfunction or spill triggers shutdown and a return to safe posture before work resumes.

records.query: Explain the risks of using the wrong lubricants and how different lubricants are applied and maintained.
records.reference: Using incorrect lubricants can accelerate degradation of non-metallic materials, leading to leakage, corrosion, electrical shorts, crazing, and mechanical failure. Lubricants must be applied using proper procedures by trained personnel. Application methods include hand or brush application, oil, squirt, or aerosol spray cans, and grease guns. Proper maintenance involves frequent washing to remove electrolytes, using noncorrosive cleaners, avoiding unauthorized chemicals, and using only approved materials for repair or replacement.
records.answer:
Risks of wrong lubricants: Not all lubricating materials are compatible with each other or with metals used in Air Force C-E-M equipment; some promote galvanic corrosion or cause paint or acrylic plastics to deteriorate, so only lubricants specified by system specific manuals/cards may be used, and failure could damage or destroy equipment or reduce mission effectiveness. Do not use greases or oils with solid film lubricants, as they are not compatible. Do not lubricate Teflon bearings or bushings; clean them with A-A-59601 (Type II or III), MIL-PRF-32295 (Type II), or MIL-PRF-680 (Type II or III) degreasing solvent. Lubricants containing graphite, alone or mixed, shall not be used because graphite is cathodic to most metals and causes galvanic corrosion in the presence of electrolytes. Do not use solid film lubricants above 1000 RPM under heavy loads or on roller bearing elements (P3257 states 1000 RPM; P2830 states 100 RPM for the same caution), and they are not suitable where relative movement is large. Use only CPCs authorized in the manual; do not use CPCs on fuel tank/cell interiors, engine fuel systems, parts above 800 F (427 C), or liquid oxygen equipment, and do not use MIL-PRF-63460 on rubber/elastomeric parts. Do not use tire lubricants containing oil or grease, which cause rapid rubber deterioration. Do not use lubricants or additives not listed in TO 36-1-7 on Air Force vehicles.

Application: Lubrication prevents wear and fills air spaces, displaces water and provides a barrier against corrosion. For hinges and pinned joints, first apply a generous quantity of MIL-PRF-63460 (preferred), MIL-PRF-81309 Type II, or MIL-PRF-32033 water-displacing CPC, actuate hinges several times, then apply the specified lubricant and wipe off excess from exterior surfaces. Apply lubricants sparingly to avoid accumulation of dust and dirt, but enough to provide adequate lubrication, wiping away excess. Apply by grease guns (lever or pressure type), oil squirt or aerosol cans, or hand/brush. Clean grease fittings (Zerk) with degreasing solvent and a clean cloth before greasing, and confirm lubricant emerges around the bushing; check fitting and gun if none appears. For flush-type high-pressure fittings, use a flush-type adapter held perpendicular to the fitting, replace the fitting if it will not accept lubricant, and wipe excess grease away. Solid film lubricants are applied over surfaces pre-coated with films such as anodize, phosphate, or epoxy primers; surface preparation is critical to wear life. MIL-PRF-46147/MIL-L-23398 cure in air (6 to 24 hours at 77 F, or accelerated by heating to 125 F for 1 to 1.5 hours after 30 minutes of air drying); SAE AS5272 (MIL-PRF-46010) requires heat cure (400 F for 1 hour Type I, 300 F for 2 hours Type II).

Maintenance: Comply with the relubrication time frame in the system specific maintenance manual. Lubricate components after cleaning operations per the system manual or lubrication charts, including door mechanisms, hinges, latches, locks, and exposed gears and bearings with an approved water-displacing lubricant to prevent corrosion, squeaking and binding. If the specified lubricant is unavailable, request substitution from the equipment SPM. For vehicles, comply with OEM intervals during warranty where they differ from Table 3-1; deviations from PM intervals require approval by 441 VSCOS AF Vehicle Management.

records.query: What causes the formation of galvanic corrosion at joints or dissimilar metal assemblies, and how can filiform corrosion be prevented in aircraft structures?
records.reference: Galvanic corrosion occurs when two dissimilar metals are in electrical contact in the presence of an electrolyte, causing the less corrosion-resistant anode to corrode faster than the more resistant cathode. Filiform corrosion can be prevented by maintaining relative humidity below 70 percent, using coatings with low rates of diffusion for oxygen and water vapors, and keeping coatings in good condition.
records.answer: Galvanic corrosion occurs when different metals are in contact with each other and an electrolyte (such as salt water); it is usually recognizable by a buildup of corrosion at the joint between the metals. The less corrosion-resistant metal (higher in the galvanic series) becomes the anode and corrodes, and the farther apart the metals are in the series, the more severe the corrosion; a small anode in contact with a large cathode corrodes much more severely. Filiform corrosion can be prevented by storing equipment and aircraft in an environment with relative humidity below 70%, using coating systems with a low rate of diffusion for oxygen and water vapors, maintaining coatings in good condition (including prompt touch-up around fasteners), washing equipment and aircraft to remove acidic contaminants from the surface, and applying corrosion preventive compounds (CPCs) when paint is damaged. Filiform corrosion starts at breaks in the coating such as scratches and cracks around fasteners and seams.

records.query: What hazards can occur during F-18 hot refueling, and what steps should be taken to minimize the risk related to tank pressure and fuel spills?
records.reference: Hazards during F-18 hot refueling include fire, fuel leaks, fuel spillage, injury or death to personnel, and long-term health hazards. Steps to minimize risk related to tank pressure and fuel spills include monitoring fuel vents on the vertical stabilizers, ensuring the bullet plug is properly aligned, securing the refueling nozzle, and avoiding hazardous areas like the tail hook zone.
records.answer: During F-18 hot refueling, the main hazards are over-pressurization and fuel spills. Monitor the fuel tank pressure indicator during refueling and stop all refueling flow if it shows red; failure to comply could result in injury, death, or long-term health hazards. Stop the hot refueling if the tank pressure gauge reaches the red zone. Do not exceed 55 PSI refueling pressure (maximum refueling pressure is 55 PSI). On F-18C/D, if the VENT TANK WET light illuminates, fuel may spill from the vent outlet(s): immediately discontinue the hot refueling. Check for airflow from the vent outlets as the tanks fill. Fuel spills are controlled by promptly stopping the operation and handling spills per local directives; a fuel spill can ignite, and any JP-4 spill must be treated as flammable. Also, if the aircraft's pre-check fails, the aircraft may only be cold refueled, and fuel must be stopped when the tanks are full, with the nozzle disconnected and the fuel shut off at the source.

records.query: State what action is required when a leak develops during refueling or defueling, and detail the emergency shutdown procedure to be followed.
records.reference: When a leak develops during refueling or defueling, stop all operations immediately. The emergency shutdown procedure is as follows: 1. Release the deadman control and pull the lanyard or control cable on the Type II hydrant system. If fuel continues to flow, actuate the nearest emergency fuel shutoff switch. 2. Actuate any of the emergency engine shutdown switches to stop the vehicle engine. 3. If the vehicle must be moved without stowing the servicing hoses or lowering the lift platform, close and disconnect the servicing nozzles and hydrant coupler, break the seal, and activate the interlock system override lever. 4. Close the hydrant coupler valve and the single-point nozzle valves. 5. Evacuate the area if instructed by maintenance or fire department personnel.
records.answer: When a leak develops during refueling or defueling, stop fuel flow and shut down the unit. Refueling emergency shutdown (TO 00-25-172CL-4, p.1-3): a. Release deadman control. b. Push engine auxiliary throttle control all the way in. c. Turn off emergency switch. d. Close hose reel shut off valve. e. Close main tank emergency shut off valve. f. Notify aircraft servicing supervisor, operations expediter and Fuels Control Center (FCC), if possible. g. Evacuate area if instructed by servicing supervisor or fire department personnel. NOTE: In case of fuel spill other than normal aircraft venting, do not evacuate fuel servicing vehicle until area is declared safe by fire department personnel. Pumping unit (R-18/R-20) emergency shutdown: a. Release deadman and activate emergency shutdown switch on hand-held remote, R-18 pumping unit, or R-20 servicing platform. b. Close R-18 inlet valve and the R-20 inlet valve (NOT the diverter valve (V27)). c. Notify aircraft servicing supervisor, operations expediter, and Fuels Service Center (FSC), if possible. d. Evacuate area if instructed by servicing supervisor or fire department personnel. Hot refueling leak/fire (TO 00-25-172): stop fuel flow, stop aircraft engines, notify the fire department, and evacuate all personnel other than fire guard(s). Defueling emergency shutdown follows the Chapter 1 Emergency Shutdown Procedures. Defueling an aircraft with a fuel leak in the system is a defueling condition requiring specific handling.

records.query: What signal is used to indicate hot brakes, and what is the first step if one is detected during inspection?
records.reference: The signal used to indicate hot brakes is to make a rapid fanning motion with one hand in front of the face while pointing to the wheel with the other hand during the day. At night, the signal is the same but with wands. The first step if hot brakes are detected during inspection is to check for hot brakes.
records.answer: Hot brakes are signaled by a rapid fanning motion with one hand in front of the face while pointing to the wheel with the other hand (day and night; same as day except with wands). If hot brakes are suspected during inspection, an aircraft hot brake check is performed prior to fuel servicing, and fuel servicing shall not start until brake temperature is below 750 oF (except A-10, C-5, C-17, C-130, E-4, F-15, and HH-60, which are exempted). Aircraft with suspected or known hot brakes will not enter the hot refueling pad.
